components.text: The decisive demand is whether missing early copies defeats historically sufficient trust, rather than merely eliminating certainty.
Whether recoverable wording requires certainty about every missing copying stage or historically adequate relative confidence.
Whether known substantial additions defeat trust in the text as a whole.
The decisive demand is what the enormous and incompletely counted raw variant total establishes about recoverability.
A secondary component concerns whether trivial spelling and word-order differences dominate the total.
Whether the enormous and incompletely counted raw variant total itself indicates unrecoverable textual instability.
Whether most recorded differences are trivial accidental variations.
The decisive demand is whether surviving witnesses within the first three centuries provide meaningful early textual access.
A further demand concerns whether missing earliest copies leaves no usable evidence of early textual states.
Whether the surviving evidence is too late and sparse to provide substantial access to early New Testament wording.
Whether collective early coverage directly reveals every intervening copying stage.
The decisive demand is whether later witnesses add useful evidence or merely multiply testimony too late to test the original.
Whether predominantly later manuscripts merely compound distance from the original rather than constrain textual growth.
Whether particular lengthy later additions nevertheless entered the tradition.
The decisive demand is whether hundreds of thousands of variants represent equally serious uncertainty.
The opposing concession that most variants are accidental and recognizable requires confirmation and specification.
Whether hundreds of thousands of differences imply correspondingly extensive meaningful textual uncertainty.
Whether most variants are accidental and normally insignificant.
The decisive demand is whether intentional or important changes create a materially large unresolved category.
Named substantial additions demonstrate that some meaningful disputes remain.
Whether a consequential subset of variants remains meaningful, viable, and interpretively material.
Whether the majority's triviality eliminates serious residual disputes.
The decisive demand is whether important textual changes threaten the trust-relevant content of the New Testament.
Substantial later additions may be influential even if no essential belief depends exclusively on them.
Whether substantial and influential additions place the text's essential theological content in jeopardy.
Whether important intentional variants can affect interpretation.
The decisive inference treats repeated copying as a serial process in which errors simply accumulate beyond recovery.
The evidentiary value of multiple witnesses depends on their ability to provide cross-checking branches.
Whether repeated copying must behave like serial degradation whose missing intermediate stages prevent reliable reconstruction.
Whether later surviving witnesses provide no useful checks on earlier textual states.
The decisive demand is whether errors in unavailable intermediate copies prevent reconstruction of an earlier exemplar.
A related issue is whether identifiable incidental errors impede reconstruction.
The harder issue of shared intentional changes remains distinct from incidental descendant errors.
Whether accumulated copying errors make reconstruction of an earlier exemplar impossible when intermediate copies are missing.
Whether identifiable incidental errors exhaust the category of consequential scribal changes.
The decisive inference moves from successful reconstruction of a surviving tradition's ancestor to recovery of the author's autograph.
The claim that an original reading survives among extant readings still requires identification of the tradition's ancestor with the autograph.
Whether successful reconstruction of the ancestor behind surviving witnesses establishes the author's original wording.
Whether editorial selection among surviving readings demonstrates autographic identity.
The decisive inference treats superiority to classical manuscript survival as evidence that the New Testament original is possessed.
More manuscripts can improve comparative reconstruction without independently identifying the autograph.
Later abundance and limited observed growth remain compatible with an earlier shared change.
Whether superiority to classical manuscript survival establishes possession of the New Testament's original wording.
Whether limited aggregate later growth demonstrates autographic identity.
The decisive demand is what degree of probabilistic continuity the surviving text supports without exact autographic knowledge.
Locating an ancestral reading among manuscripts does not determine exact identity with Mark's wording.
Whether a probabilistic rather than certainty standard establishes sufficient confidence in exact or substantial textual continuity.
Whether branching checks exclude complete discontinuity while leaving the degree of difference uncertain.
The decisive demand is whether actual first- and second-century copying and exemplars were reliable enough for trust.
A shared early ancestor still requires evidence concerning that ancestor's quality and relation to earlier copying.
A relative-confidence standard still requires affirmative evidence sufficient to meet the proposed trust threshold.
Whether the advocate supplied affirmative evidence that first- and second-century copying and exemplars were sufficiently reliable.
Whether P75 and Vaticanus establish the quality of still earlier exemplars.
Whether defining trust as relative confidence eliminates the need for affirmative early-transmission evidence.
The decisive demand is what evidentiary standard the advocate of trust must meet for an ancient text.
Both sides accept probability, leaving the question whether broad historical confidence can support trust.
Ancestral-versus-autographic distinction limits certainty but need not eliminate historically warranted probability.
Whether trust in an ancient text should require radical certainty about inaccessible early copying or ordinary historical probability.
Whether a probability standard alone specifies the degree of textual continuity achieved.
Whether probabilistic historical trust eliminates the ancestor-versus-autograph distinction.
